newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn plans sale of oil reserves by end 1999, sources say.
newsitem.headline: Bonn plans sale of oil reserves by end 1999, sources say.

text.p: Germany plans to sell off its entire strategic reserves of 7.3 million tons of crude oil by late 1999 to help cut the budget deficit and qualify for Europe's single currency, government sources said Friday.

The sources said the sale of the reserves stockpiled since the late 1970s -- expected to bring in around 1.4 billion marks ($798 million) in total to the government's empty coffers -- would take place in stages and should be completed by the end of 1999.
They said Bonn planned to sell a first instalment of its reserves -- 2.8 million barrels of crude oil -- in the next few weeks. Details of the sale will be made public next week.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet approved part of the sale Friday when it passed a supplementary budget for 1997 and a draft 1998 budget which include plans to sell 400 million marks ($228 million) of crude this year and 500 million marks ($285 million) in 1998 to help fill yawning budget gaps.

At current oil prices, 400 million marks of oil would be at least 75,000 barrels per day for the rest of this year -- roughly equivalent to the output of a medium-sized North Sea field -- being pushed onto a market already beginning to buckle under the weight of rising supply.

Brent crude oil, the world benchmark, was trading at $17.96 Friday morning -- about $1 below levels at the start of July on news that Iraq may be edging towards a resumption of limited oil exports under a U.N. oil-for-food accord.
Germany's planned sales amount to just a tenth of that expected from Iraq, but oil traders and analysts said the move was likely to hit prices in a weak market.
"The German move is yet another blow to an already bearish market," said John Toalster of SGST Securities.
"The volumes of crude from Germany are relatively small but the fundamentals are finely balanced," Paul Spedding of Kleinwort Benson in London said.

Germany's concern, however, is with the control of a ballooning budget deficit expected to surge to 71 billion marks ($40.5 billion) this year, up from an original plan of 53.3 billion ($30.4 billion), hurting its hopes of joining economic and monetary union.

The Paris-based International Energy Agency, which was established by major industrial nations after the 1974 oil price shock to protect its 24 members against future crises, slammed the German plans.
Under emergency reserve obligations signed in 1975, IEA members are required to hold at least 90 days of net imports and release oil in the event of serious market turmoil.
But even if Bonn dumps its entire strategic crude oil stock, reserves held on behalf of German oil companies would still meet the agency's minimum requirement.

Germany is Europe's most oil-import dependent economy, relying on foreign supplies for 97 percent of consumption. Last year, it imported 2.1 million barrels per day of crude and about 650,000 bpd of refined products like gasoline and heating oil.
